clue.text: Unhealthy American, not right, lacking energy

indicators.note: something unhealthy is in poor shape, so the letters left are put into a new order
not right says the letter for right is taken out of the word before it

explanation.surface: A sickly American visitor, out of sorts and short of pep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unhealthy' looks like the definition but is the anagram signal; AMERICAN without its R leaves AMEICAN, which 'Unhealthy' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Anaemia, a shortage of red blood cells, leaves a person pale and tired, so the adjective describes feeble, listless things.

clue.text: A new faculty head from the highlands?

parts.note: a dean heads a university faculty

explanation.surface: Is a newly appointed head of faculty a Scottish Highlander?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: the Andes are one set of highlands, so this is a narrower sense than 'Scottish'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes people or things from the Andes mountains of South America, one example of high country.

clue.text: Coming back through Soho, I gad about at a slow pace

indicators.note: coming back says the letters are read from right to left
the answer runs through the words Soho, I gad about, spanning them

explanation.surface: Someone wandering back through Soho, strolling idly about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'through' marks letters running across 'Soho, I gad a(bout)'; 'Coming back' reads them from right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: In music the Italian tempo marking means slowly, so it serves as an adverb for leisurely pace.

clue.text: Banks of money going to Panama? I don't believe it!

indicators.note: banks are the edges of a river, so the outer letters of the next word are taken

parts.note: a Panama is a kind of straw hat

explanation.surface: Someone astonished that bank funds are being moved to Panama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Panama' suggests the country and a tax haven; here it is the straw hat.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a dated exclamation of surprise or disbelief, like 'well I never!'

clue.text: Polar coords carved on roundabout sign, indicating US location

indicators.note: in a down entry on means the first part sits above the next
carved suggests cut up and reshaped, so these letters are rearranged
roundabout means turned about, so the four letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Map coordinates etched onto a road sign at a traffic circle, showing an American place.
explanation.walkthrough: Two anagrams: 'carved' rearranges POLAR COORDS; 'roundabout' rearranges SIGN, which follows.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a city in the state at the foot of Pikes Peak, a place in America.

clue.text: Cast down — failing to get justice for fellow

indicators.note: to get one letter in place of another signals a swap within the word
for marks which letter is being replaced

parts.note: a failing is a flaw or shortcoming
J is the abbreviation for justice, as in a judge's title

explanation.surface: Someone downcast after missing out on justice for a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The flaw word has its F (fellow) swapped for J (justice).
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to depress or dishearten, which is what casting someone down does.

clue.text: RC officials have been turning down case studies, primarily involving mischief

definitions.text: RC officials have been turning down case studies, primarily involving mischief

parts.words: RC officials have been turning down case studies, primarily involving mischief
parts.note: the Catholic office whose holders argued against causes for sainthood, so their job was opposing each case, and the title puts the devil in charge

explanation.surface: Church officials rejecting candidacies whose evidence smacks of mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: The Promoter of the Faith argued against each candidate for canonisation; the role's popular title names the Devil, the prime source of mischief.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase was the popular title of Vatican officials who argued against proposed saints, now anyone arguing the contrary side.

clue.text: Jane's offer is out of order after ignoring a president

indicators.note: being out of order means jumbled, so the remaining letters are rearranged
ignoring the letter a means it is dropped from the words before

explanation.surface: Jane's proposal gets ruled out of order for snubbing a head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring a' drops one A from JANES OFFER; 'is out of order' rearranges JNESOFFER.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas of that surname was the third head of state of the United States.

clue.text: Axe murder cases never fail to make an impression

indicators.note: cases means encloses, so the pair surrounds the other word

parts.note: to axe something is to cut it
ice is slang for kill
no can mean never, as in 'no way'

explanation.surface: Axe murder trials always leave a deep impression on the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cases' looks like court cases but is the container signal. Ice meaning kill is American gangster slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes having no effect or influence on someone, the opposite of impressing them.

clue.text: Ballet impresario lived unhappily with one hag

indicators.note: unhappily suggests things going wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one

explanation.surface: A dance promoter shares a miserable home with an old crone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unhappily' rearranges LIVED, I (one) and HAG.
explanation.definitionFit: Sergei of that name founded the Ballets Russes, the great Russian dance company in Paris.

clue.text: Escort stripped off to make an impression

indicators.note: stripped means the outer letters are peeled away, leaving the middle

parts.note: to etch is to engrave, leaving a mark in a surface

explanation.surface: An escort who undresses to make a good first impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' stripped of its outer letters leaves F; 'stripped off' reads as undressing.
explanation.definitionFit: To escort someone can mean to go and bring them, which is what the verb meaning collect describes.

clue.text: Whetstone after splitting open

parts.note: split into whet and stone: whet gives hone, and stone gives its abbreviation st

explanation.surface: A sharpening stone that has cracked open.
explanation.walkthrough: Split WHETSTONE into WHET and STONE: to whet is to HONE, and ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight of 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: An open person is frank and candid, hiding nothing, which is the adjective's sense.

clue.text: A pilot once discovered a sex toy after clearing out bedroom

indicators.note: clearing out means the abbreviation for bedroom is removed from the word

parts.note: a vibrator is a sex toy
BR is the abbreviation for bedroom in property ads

explanation.surface: An old-time airman stumbles on a sex toy while tidying the bedroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after clearing out' removes the bedroom abbreviation used in British estate agents' listings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word for a flyer of aircraft is now somewhat old-fashioned, hence 'once'.

clue.text: Before noon, Oscar Wilde went off for a quick nap

indicators.note: went off suggests something going bad, so the letters of the name are rearranged

parts.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: before here means the start of the word, its opening letter

explanation.surface: Oscar Wilde dozed off for forty winks before midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'went off' rearranges WILDE with O (Oscar) and N, the first letter of 'noon'.
explanation.definitionFit: A short rest on a bed or sofa is a brief nap, the hyphenated noun's meaning.

clue.text: German father's laundered cash for US bankers

parts.note: old man is a slang term for father, here possessive

indicators.note: laundered cash is cleaned and reworked, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A German dad's dirty money passed through the American banking system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laundered' rearranges CASH to SACHS, after G and OLD MAN'S.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a major Wall Street investment bank, a firm of financiers in the United States.

clue.text: United spent lolly without using heads, recklessly and lavishly

indicators.note: recklessly suggests wild and careless, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names

indicators.note: without heads means each word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: A football club splashing out its money carelessly and extravagantly.
explanation.walkthrough: SPENT and LOLLY lose their first letters, leaving PENTOLLY; 'recklessly' rearranges these with U. LOLLY is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in a rich, luxurious manner is to do it with extravagance.

clue.text: Clever, posh females admitted being soft and light

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: fly is British slang for sharp or clever
U stands for upper-class, so posh
FF is the plural abbreviation for females

explanation.surface: Smart posh women let into something downy and airy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitted' signals the container. U for posh comes from the old British U and non-U class labels.
explanation.definitionFit: Something downy and feathery is soft and light, like a cloud or a kitten's coat.

clue.text: Strange Fruit, mainly penned by suggestion of Adam Ant

indicators.note: penned by means enclosed by the other letters
a suggestion is a hint, so just the first letter of the name is used
mainly means most of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: a berry is a fruit

explanation.surface: Strange Fruit, the song, rewritten by the pop star Adam Ant on a whim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mainly' trims the fruit, 'suggestion of' takes one letter of Adam, and 'penned by' signals the container. Adam Ant was a 1980s British pop star.
explanation.definitionFit: Something odd departs from the norm, which is the sense of deviating.

clue.text: It's so efficient to have party at bar

parts.note: Labour is a major British political party
bar and saving can both mean except

explanation.surface: Having a party at the pub saves effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' looks like the pub but means 'except', as does SAVING. LABOUR is Britain's main left-wing party.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadget that reduces the work needed is efficient at sparing human effort.

clue.text: People changing sides regularly tend to be deceitful

indicators.note: changing sides swaps left for right, the letter for one side becoming the other

parts.note: folk means people

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: People who keep switching allegiance are seen as untrustworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: In FOLK, L (left) is swapped for R (right), giving FORK; alternate letters of 'tend' give ED.
explanation.definitionFit: A forked tongue is the mark of a liar, so the adjective means deceitful.

clue.text: Maybe Reading University will block film course

indicators.note: to block something is to sit inside and fill it, so these letters go inside

parts.note: a skin is a thin film, as on custard
reading is one of the three Rs, so it may be R

explanation.surface: Reading University stops a movie course from running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reading' looks like the English university town but is one of the three Rs (reading, writing and arithmetic), hence 'Maybe'.
explanation.definitionFit: A slope marked out for skiing is a course on the mountain.

clue.text: Refrain from anxiety when catching ball

indicators.note: catching means holding inside, so one word goes into the other

parts.note: fear is anxiety
an orb is a ball or sphere

explanation.surface: Steering clear of nerves while trying to catch a ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refrain' looks like a noun, a chorus, but here it is the verb; 'when catching' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold back from doing something is to abstain or show restraint, the verb's meaning.

clue.text: Early riser catches fool in clerical attire

indicators.note: catches means holds within, so one word goes inside

parts.note: the cockerel crows at dawn, so it is an early riser
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: An early-rising priest catches a fool wearing church robes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early riser' sounds like a person but is the cockerel; 'catches' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, close-fitting garment worn by clergy and choristers is church dress.

clue.text: Son gets off craft

parts.note: to off someone is slang for to kill them

explanation.surface: A son disembarks from a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' looks like a vessel to get off, but it means expertise; 'off' is slang for kill.
explanation.definitionFit: Craft as expertise or dexterity means ability at a task.

clue.text: Still with old copper lining that's used when making whisky

indicators.note: lining means sitting inside, so these letters go within the other word

parts.note: still and yet both mean even so
the as was an ancient Roman copper coin

explanation.surface: A whisky still lined with old copper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like a distilling still but is an adverb; 'lining' signals the container. The as was a Roman coin.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the fungus that ferments the sugars in the mash, producing alcohol for distillation.

clue.text: Egg's best served with endless butter for fussy type

parts.note: a nit is the egg of a louse; the 's means 'is'
the pick of something is the best of it

indicators.note: endless takes the butt off the word, a butt being an end

explanation.surface: The best egg, served with plenty of butter, for a picky eater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' plays on butt meaning end: BUTTER without BUTT leaves ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who finds fault with trivial details is a pedant, a fussy person.

clue.text: Railroads blown apart by your old radicals

indicators.note: being blown apart means opened up, so the other letters sit inside

parts.note: els are elevated railways in US cities
thy is the old form of your

explanation.surface: Railway lines bombed by your old revolutionary radicals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'radicals' looks political but is chemistry: the C2H5 group. ELS, short for elevated railways, is American.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry a radical is a group of atoms that acts as a unit, as this two-carbon group does.

clue.text: Old Kurdish leader perhaps leaves home

parts.note: leaves such as lettuce make a salad, an example signalled by perhaps
in means at home

explanation.surface: An old Kurdish chief possibly departs for home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' looks like a verb, departing, but is salad greens.
explanation.definitionFit: The twelfth-century sultan who fought the Crusaders was of Kurdish origin, a famous historic ruler.
